A meme product looks trivial until you try to make it repeatable. "Turn a photo into the viral Get a Job clip" sounds like one model call. It is a queue, a template, and a consent policy.

##  The joke is the template, not the model

What makes a meme recognisable is the **fixed structure** : the same framing, the same timing, the same punchline shape. Once you accept that, the build stops being "choose a model" and becomes "define the template precisely enough that any input lands in the same format".

That means the interesting engineering is in the constraints:

  1. **One input.** A photo. Not a prompt, not a paragraph, not a set of settings.
  2. **A fixed duration.** Memes are short because attention is the scarce thing.
  3. **A predictable first second.** If the opening frame is not obviously "the joke", nothing after it matters.



##  Consent is a product decision, not a legal footnote

Making a video of a real person raises questions that a checkbox does not answer. The version that people were comfortable sharing had three things:

  * a plain statement of who the photo must be
  * a plain statement of what happens to the file
  * a visible way to start over



None of that is model work. All of it is why the thing felt usable.

##  Generation is slow — design the wait

Every image-to-video tool underestimates the perceived wait. Progress that names what is happening beats a spinner; a result you can download immediately beats a beautiful result you have to hunt for.

If you are documenting one of these tools, write the image to video workspace page around the constraints, not the model.

_Written after shipping a deliberately constrained first version._
external.title: Turning a meme into a product: what actually has to be built

external.description:
I build SpaceApp, a self-hosted workspace for running AI coding CLIs in isolated rooms. A room organizes work; each pane in it is an independent CLI or app session. The runtimes on offer are OpenCode, Codex, Gemini, Qwen Code, Kimi Code, Grok Build and an experimental DeepSeek CLI; Claude Code has its own owner-initiated installation flow.

The latest setup releases were about one stretch of the experience: the time between running the installer and getting a first useful answer. Here is that path step by step, and what changed on it.

##  1. Install

You need Linux, macOS or Windows 11, Node.js 20.11 or newer, and at least 4 CPUs, 8 GB RAM and 15 GiB of free disk. The standard profile, which adds a managed browser, recommends 8 CPUs, 16 GB RAM and 25 GiB.



    npx --yes run-spaceapp@latest install


The launcher manages the core API and web app, the CLI runtimes, PostgreSQL and Temporal. The default light profile leaves out the managed Chromium; the standard profile starts a browser container as well.

##  2. Create the owner account

Once the installation passes its readiness checks, you use a one-time setup token to create the first account, register the folders you want agents to work in, and connect providers through their official login flows or masked credential input.

Host folders are visible only after you register them as workspaces, and read-only mounts are supported.

**New:** the setup wizard's Ready step offers three first prompts you can copy.

##  3. The first model

The first OpenCode pane starts on a free model, Big Pickle. A model counts as working only after a real tool call: it has to read a small file with its read tool and answer with the random token inside it. When Big Pickle fails that check, the newest free tool-capable models are tried instead.

Free models can change upstream at any time. If the one you are on stops responding, pick another in OpenCode.

##  4. The first prompt

Two things used to get in the way here.

**A room without a project had nowhere obvious to write.** Now a CLI pane in such a room starts in `/workspaces/<room>`, so a first prompt like "build me a page" writes `index.html` there.

**The first task could stop at a permission prompt.** On macOS, a first OpenCode task could wait at "Access external directory /tmp" until someone answered. Now OpenCode's first run authorizes only its own private scratch directory, and the bootstrap instructions send temporary files there. Other paths outside the workspace still ask.

##  5. Staying current

The app now shows "Update available" when a newer release exists and opens the update command with a Copy button:



    npx --yes run-spaceapp@latest update


##  What to know before you try it

  * SpaceApp is designed for one trusted owner on one self-hosted instance.
  * Backups are portable and checksummed and cover application data, PostgreSQL and owner memory. Provider credentials, login state, workspace contents and browser profiles are left out.
  * Telemetry is opt-in. Answer No and nothing is sent. Answer Yes and one anonymous event is sent the first time an agent finishes an answer (event, random id, version, CPU architecture, date).



##  Feedback welcome

I would like to hear where the first five minutes still break for you: your OS, the profile the installer picked, and the step where it stopped. The full release notes are here: https://github.com/oll4com/spaceapp/releases
external.title: From one command to a first page: what changed in SpaceApp's setup

external.description: Plants seem stationary: they don’t skip, fly or walk around. But that doesn’t mean they don’t move. The organisms bend their roots and shoots in response to stimuli such as water, light, salt and gravity. These responsive movements, called tropisms, are crucial for plants’ survival. Now researchers have discovered a new way plants move, which they call “saprotropism”: the bending of roots to avoid dead or rotting plant tissue. The results were published in Science. The discovery began with a failed experiment and an unexpected observation. Yuzhou Zhang, a biologist at Northwest A&F University in China, was studying how plants move in response to gravity in a laboratory in Austria when one of his agar plates became contaminated with airborne microbes. Just before he threw it away, he noticed something striking: almost every single one of the plants’ roots in the plate was bent away from the spoilage. The consistency “immediately made me wonder whether this was more than a random response,” Zhang says. external.description: The task: turn documents into structured data Many business workflows need to turn documents into structured data. The model must find the right values, capture the requested records, and return output the next system can use. Long documents and repeated tables make this harder. We tested gpt-oss-20b and gpt-oss-120b to explore lower-cost alternatives to frontier models. In our baseline tests, both fell short on field coverage. gpt-oss-20b also declined the task or returned unparseable output. We wanted to see whether task-specific fine-tuning could improve these results. In Figure 1, we show an invoice that we held out from training. We can quickly spot the invoice number, customer, due date, and balance, but our application must map those values to the correct schema fields, preserve all 37 line items, and return complete, valid JSON. A wrong or missing value can trigger downstream errors or manual review, while invalid JSON can break the workflow altogether. Figure 1. Reconstructed excerpt from a public held-out invoice. Highlighted spans show representative values the model must find; the full evaluation uses the complete document and schema. We used schema-guided extraction. We gave the model document text and a JSON Schema defining the required fields, then asked it to return one JSON object. Our grader compared normalized field-path/value pairs with the expected answer, counting repeated occurrences. We measure precision as the share of extracted pairs that match the expected answer, and recall as the share of expected pairs we recover correctly. We use F1 to combine the two into one score, using their harmonic mean. F1 ranges from 0 to 1, with higher scores indicating better extraction. A wrong value hurts precision and can also hurt recall if the expected value remains unmatched. A missing value hurts recall. What changed after fine-tuning We evaluated the base and fine-tuned versions of gpt-oss-20b and gpt-oss-120b on the same 20 documents. Both improved their extraction F1. gpt-oss-20b rose from 0.4379 to 0.8115, and gpt-oss-120b rose from 0.6816 to 0.8573. gpt-oss-20b made the larger gain, with an 85.3% relative improvement after 100 GRPO steps. Fine-tuned gpt-oss-120b finished with the higher F1. Fine-tuning helped both models, but the size of the improvement differed. We also evaluated GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6-sol, and GPT-6-sol as reference models. They scored 0.9760, 0.9766, and 0.9764, respectively—still higher than our fine-tuned models. gpt-oss-20b reached 83.1% of GPT-5.6-sol’s reference F1. This is a substantial improvement for gpt-oss-20b and a promising starting point for further task-specific tuning. Our base and tuned scores are averaged across repeated evaluations, while the reference models used a different single-pass protocol. These reference scores provide useful context for the progress we made, with the evaluation differences noted above. Figure 2. Macro F1 for gpt-oss-20b and gpt-oss-120b before and after fine-tuning on the same 20 documents, with frontier models as references. Base and tuned scores average repeated evaluations; frontier references use a different single-pass protocol. These improvements make lower inference-cost base models worth a closer look. Table 1 compares published Azure inference prices. The pricing comparison is intended to provide inference-cost context only and should not be interpreted as a complete total-cost-of-ownership analysis, which would also include training, hosting, retries, and operational costs. Table 1. Extraction macro F1 and published Azure inference prices (USD per 1M tokens); GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6-sol, and GPT-6-sol are included as frontier-model references Model Macro F1 Azure input / 1M Azure output / 1M gpt-oss-20b 0.8115 $0.07 $0.30 gpt-oss-120b 0.8573 $0.15 $0.60 GPT-5.6-sol 0.9766 $4.00 $20.00 GPT-5.5 0.9760 $5.00 $30.00 GPT-6-sol 0.9764 $2.00 $10.00 Notes: Prices checked October 9, 2026, in USD; input rates are uncached. gpt-oss-20b prices are published fine-tuned inference rates for Regional deployments. gpt-oss-120b prices are base-model rates; its fine-tuned rates remain unconfirmed. Frontier prices use Global Standard pricing, with the short-context tier for GPT-5.6-sol and GPT-6-sol. These rates do not represent measured deployment costs for our experimental checkpoints. Token rates exclude training and hosting costs. F1 scores come from fine-tuned checkpoints for the two gpt-oss models and reference runs for the frontier models. All use the same 20 documents, but tuned scores average repeated evaluations while frontier references use a different single-pass protocol. We observed more parseable output and higher coverage We looked through gpt-oss-20b’s responses and found examples where it declined the task or said it could not finish. We tracked this with a “refusal-wording rate”: the share of responses where our grader detected an apology or cannot-complete language. This measures wording, not whether the model made a safety refusal. We tracked JSON parseability and field coverage separately, although these problems can overlap. After fine-tuning, the refusal-wording rate (Refusals) fell from 25% to zero; JSON parseability (Valid JSON) rose from 63.8% to 98.8%, and coverage rose from 47.1% to 94.9%. Valid JSON means our grader could read the response as an object or array. Coverage compares the number of predicted field/value pairs with the expected count, capped at 100%. Wrong or extra pairs can raise coverage, so we read it alongside F1 rather than treat it as a measure of correctness. Figure 3. Extraction quality and output behavior before and after fine-tuning on the same 20 documents. Bars show means across repeated evaluations. “Valid JSON” measures JSON parseability, not schema compliance or value correctness. “Refusal rate” measures detected refusal wording, not safety refusals. Higher is better except for refusal rate. Figure 4 shows how these measures changed during training. We repeated the full training run with a second seed. It reached 0.8101 F1, close to the headline run’s 0.8115. We ran four temperature-0 evaluations for each seed. Across all eight post-training evaluations, our grader detected no refusal wording. Figure 4. gpt-oss-20b’s training progress, evaluated on 20 documents held out from training. (A) Refusal-wording rate falls as JSON parseability and field coverage improve. (B) Macro F1 rises and then levels off. Error bars show standard deviation across four temperature-0 evaluations. What we learned from the model comparison We saw different starting points and different gains between the two models. gpt-oss-20b had clearer output problems before training: it sometimes declined the task, returned unparseable JSON, or missed required information. After fine-tuning, we saw improvements in extraction F1, JSON parseability, and field coverage, along with less refusal wording. gpt-oss-120b started with fewer format problems. We detected no refusal wording, and 96.3% of its baseline responses were parseable JSON. But parseable output did not mean complete or correct extraction. After fine-tuning, its field coverage rose from 74.1% to 94.1%, and its F1 rose from 0.6816 to 0.8573. gpt-oss-20b made the larger F1 gain, while fine-tuned gpt-oss-120b finished with the higher F1. For us, the lesson is to measure the problem first. Try simpler, lower-cost changes, such as prompting, before committing to training. Then consider fine-tuning when your grader can reward the improvements your application needs. How we trained with Foundry Interactive Training We used the Foundry Interactive Training API [1] with 17 training documents, expected structured answers, and a Python grader. We followed the cookbook to connect our grader to Foundry’s managed generation and training operations. We ran 100 group relative policy optimization, or GRPO, steps and saved checkpoints for evaluation. For each document, we had gpt-oss-20b generates eight candidate answers. Our grader awarded partial credit for correct values and penalized invalid JSON. GRPO used the candidates’ relative scores to reinforce better answers. We used the expected answers only for grading. We did not include them in the inputs we gave the model during reinforcement training. The model had to produce its own answers, and the grader supplied the feedback. Figure 5. Customers define the application outcome and quality bar; Foundry Interactive Training runs the post-training loop in Microsoft Foundry. How customers can use Foundry Interactive Training To try this approach, bring four ingredients: a supported base model, examples from your workload, expected outcomes, or another way to check the answers, and a Python grader. Your grader should measure what matters to the application—not just whether an answer looks convincing. Get connected. Request access to the Microsoft Foundry Interactive Training public preview [2] and connect the onboarding cookbook [3][4] to an assigned Foundry project. Separate your data. Build training, validation, and final test sets. Use validation data to choose checkpoints. Keep the final test set for an independent check, with new sources and document structures where possible. Build your grader. Implement a grader that rewards the desired outcome. For our extraction task, we checked normalized field-path/value pairs and penalized unparseable JSON. Run a bounded experiment. Set a training budget, inspect the training signal, and compare saved checkpoints on the validation set. Once you choose a checkpoint, evaluate it on the untouched final test set. Evaluate and prepare for deployment. Use session sampling to test your LoRA adapter on held-out prompts and compare it with the baseline. Save checkpoints so you can continue experimenting. Before using the model in an application, confirm the supported deployment path, model compatibility, and serving costs. Takeaway With Foundry Interactive Training, we improved extraction F1 for both gpt-oss-20b and gpt-oss-120b. We brought our task examples and a Python grader, and Foundry managed the generation and training loop. gpt-oss-20b made the larger gain, while fine-tuned gpt-oss-120b reached the higher F1. We did not match the frontier references, but our results show why task-specific fine-tuning is worth exploring before switching to a higher-priced model. The final choice should depend on independently tested quality and the full cost of deployment. Reference [1] https://github.com/microsoft-foundry/fine-tuning [2] What is interactive training (preview) in Microsoft Foundry? - Microsoft Foundry | Microsoft Learn [3] Interactive Training - Public Preview Intake Form [4] https://github.com/microsoft-foundry/fine-tuning/tree/main/interactive_training

record.text: AI Medicine is on the horizon. How it’s designed will shape how patients feel about it, and whether they trust it at all.

external.description:
My doctor’s office is telling new patients to expect a seven-month wait. That’s not a typo.

**Seven.**

By the time an appointment opens up, the weather will have turned twice. Clinics near me keep closing, and the ones still open seem short on everything, especially time.

I don’t think this is just a rurual-ish Virginia problem. I think it’s the first chapter of a much bigger story, and AI is about to play a large part in it.

## The Numbers Behind the Long Wait

The Association of American Medical Colleges projects that the U.S. will be short between 13,500 and 86,000 physicians by 2036. Part of the reason for that shortage will be age. The same report says 20% of clinical physicians are 65 or older, and another 22% are between 55 and 64. A big share of the workforce is close to retirement, and I can only imagine that the situations they are and will be in are making retirement feel more and more like a viable option.

The doctors still working are stretched. The AMA found that 41.9% of physicians reported at least one symptom of burnout in 2025. That was better than 48.2% in 2023. That’s about four out of ten. In family medicine, the specialty most of us rely on, the figure is 45%.

More patients, fewer doctors. Something has to give.

## Your Watch Is Already Doing Part of a Doctor’s Job

Apple’s hypertension notifications received FDA clearance in September 2025. The watch tracks how your blood vessels respond to each heartbeat over 30 days and alerts you if the pattern points to high blood pressure. Apple expects it to flag more than a million people with undiagnosed hypertension in the first year.

It doesn’t take a blood pressure reading, and the FDA treats the alert as a reason for more testing rather than a diagnosis. Apple also says the feature isn’t meant for people under 22, people already diagnosed with hypertension, or pregnant users. Even so, a screening that used to mean booking an appointment now happens on your wrist.

## AI Trained Only on Medicine Is Already Being Tested

At EPRI, I’m working on a model trained on energy. I expect someone is building the same kind of thing for medicine.

external.description:
I've been building a news and magazine theme called Acta Cosmica, and it's now available in two versions: Astro and Ghost. Here's an overview of each, and where to get them.

## The Idea Behind Acta Cosmica

Inspired by National Geographic, Acta Cosmica is designed for online publishers, independent journalists, niche digital newsrooms, and content-driven media brands who want to publish with the polish of a real newsroom and convert readers into loyal subscribers and members.

I started with the Astro version, then converted it into a native Ghost theme so subscriber conversion is built on Ghost's own memberships, comments, and newsletters instead of bolted on after the fact.

## Acta Cosmica for Astro

The original build was made with Astro 7. It's a fully static, SEO-ready theme with a config-driven category system: you can swap the demo's science/nature sections for your own beats by editing a single data file, no template changes required. Each category automatically gets its own subcategory filter chips, and the homepage's spotlight rows can be reordered or reassigned the same way.

Photos get automatic WebP conversion and responsive srcset sizing, so there's no manual resizing as you publish. Articles are managed through Astro Content Collections with schema-validated Markdown, and the nav, footer, authors, categories, and About-page copy all live in editable TypeScript data files rather than component code.

Design-wise, it leans into an editorial broadsheet look: warm cream backgrounds against near-black ink, a single configurable accent color, Archivo for display type, and Newsreader (a literary serif) for body copy. It ships with a full page set, homepage, category pages, article pages, author profiles, a writers directory, About, Membership, Contact, Search (with weighted fuzzy matching and a ⌘K shortcut), saved stories, an account page, legal pages, and a custom 404.

Built on Astro 7, Tailwind CSS v4, TypeScript, and vanilla JS, with no client-side JS framework required.

## Acta Cosmica for Ghost

The Ghost conversion keeps the same photo-forward storytelling and typographic design, but wires everything into Ghost 5.0.0+, so membership, comments, search, and newsletters all run natively instead of needing to be wired up separately.

  * **Fully configurable category system** — categories are Ghost tags; nav, footer, and homepage spotlight rows are driven by theme settings and Ghost's navigation, no template edits needed
  * **Native Ghost membership & paywall** — free/members-only/paid post gating with a branded subscribe CTA; tier pricing pulls live from Settings > Membership
  * **Native comments, search, and newsletters** — Ghost's built-in commenting, a custom weighted full-text search overlay (⌘K shortcut), and newsletter signup wired to Ghost's newsletter feature
  * **Full Koenig editor card support** — bookmark, gallery, callout, toggle, button, header cards, plus a fully custom before/after image-comparison card
  * **Reader UX extras** — a reading progress bar, a writers directory with live story counts, and a branded 404 page



**Pages included:** homepage (hero, latest-stories rail, category spotlight rows, photo-of-the-day, Editor's Pick/Most Read), article page with paywall CTA and related stories, membership page with live tier pricing, writers directory, category/tag archives, author profiles, branded 404, and legal pages.

**Built on:** Ghost 5.0.0+, Tailwind CSS v4, Google Fonts (Archivo + Newsreader), hand-tuned inline SVG icons, vanilla JS, and SEO via Ghost's own `{{ghost_head}}` output.

a view of Staunton, VA

When I wrote about my location-based gamification app Markur last summer, the platform was an exploratory experiment more than a working product. It had promise, and the bones were solid. The first version was taken offline in August 2025 as I rethought the structure and purpose. There were too many open questions. Is this a privacy concern? How hard will this be to maintain? How expensive will it be to keep up? Will people even... _use it_?

The months since have answered most of those questions.

QCMM.app is the proof of concept Markur always needed. It's a location-based discovery and community app built around **Queen City Magic & Mischief**, a festival coming to downtown Staunton, Virginia each September. The app maps over 119 locations across the city's historic core, giving festival-goers a way to explore, check in, and connect before, during, and after the event. It runs on a rebuilt version of the Markur platform, now formally rebranded as **Markur.app** , and the gap between what the first version was and what this one is, is significant.

* * *

## Starting Over the Right Way

The original Markur was a generalist platform. Location-based, yes, but pointed at everything and therefore aimed at nothing. QCMM.app took the opposite approach. One city. One festival. One tightly scoped set of locations to explore.
